Plaintiff's suit, is that, the suit land was acquired by defendant No. 1 by his own fund for his benefit, but some of the deeds were registered in the names of his sons, daughters and wife named, Nasir Uddin Harji, Nazli Hasan, Nostan Hirji and Mrs. Noor Sultan Hirji respectively. In the plaint it has been stated that defendant No. 1 being the ostensible owner of the land in suit, with the consent of his above named son, daughters and wife entered into an agreement to sell the land in suit on 21-11-1996 with the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 90,00,000 (ninety lakh), which is the price of 20 bighas of land measured at 30 decimals per bigha, rate of which was at Taka 4,50,000 per bigha and received Taka 10,00,000 (Ten lakh) by cheque No. 15588 dated 21-11-1996 and he gave a signed receipt of the said money. Later on, on the back side of said bainapatra, he acknowledge further receipt of Taka 20 lakh on 10-12-96 and an agreement was entered for performance of the contract. On 21-11-1996, defendant No. 1 informed the plaintiff that the necessary documents and Khatians were not in his hand and for this reason it was not possible to mention the required dag numbers and Khatian numbers in the bainapatra and made commitment to furnish a fresh bainapatra in writing with dag numbers and Khatian numbers later on at a convenient time. The defendant No. 1 also informed plaintiff No. 1 that as his daughter resides in Canada, sons are to much busy in their business and his wife is 'pardanashin' lady, verbally all of them have agreed to deliver their portion of land by virtue of general power of attorney to him to sell their respective proportionate share of the suit land. The plaintiff sincerely believed defendant No. 1 very much and frankly entered into contract for sale by writing the above mentioned Bonaparte and gave Taka 30,00,000 (thirty lakh) to defendant No. 1 in two installments. It is further plaintiff's case that, the sons and daughter of defendant No. 1 furnished the said general power to attorney in favour of defendant No. 1 to sell their respective shares of the suit land which in benami was owned by them. It is further plaintiff's case that, on receipt of the 2nd installment of Taka 20,00,000, defendant committed to draw up a formal agreement between him and Messrs Metropolitan Builders, represented by the plaintiff.

Learned Advocate in support of his sub-missions, relied on the decision of Nasima Akhter vs Md Siraj Miah, 10 MLR (AD) 53 = 57 DLR (AD) 38 where it has been held that, "It is well settled that time is not essence of the contract for sale of immovable property. When the execution of the deed of agreement is proved but tendering of the balance consideration is not proved the High Court Division in appeal granted higher amount of consideration above that settled in the bainanama as solatium to the defendant". Learned Advocate next relied on the case of Hajee Lal Miah vs Nurul Amin, 10 MLR (AD) 249 = 57 DLR (AD) 64 where it has been held that, 'Where in a case the plaintiff proved the genuineness of contract for sale of immovable property and the subsequent transferee purchasing the same land with knowledge of the previous contract, the contract may be enforced against the subsequent transferee as contemplated under section 27 of the Specific Relief Act." Learned Advocate next relief on in the case of Joynab Begum vs Shaheb Ali Akunji, reported in 12 MLR 337 where it has been held "Section 27(b)-Provides for specific performance of contract as against the person making the contract and also against subsequent transferee except the bonafide purchaser for valuable consideration without notice of the original agreement. The onus is upon the subsequent purchaser that he purchased the said land in good faith and paid the consideration and he had no knowledge of the original agreement." Learned Advocate next relied on decision of Shamsul Haque vs Sarajat A reported in 46 DLR 57 where it has been held that, 'Mr Abdur Rashid also argued that the lower appellate Court committed a serious error in law in its decision in finding possession of the defendants although the defendants did not specifically deny the allegation of possession of the plaintiffs by filing written statement or pleading." Learned Advocate next relied on decision of Reliable Jute Traders vs Sonali Bank reported in 7 BLC 16 where it has been held that, "Rule 2 of Order VI of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that pleadings must contain all material facts, while rule 3 of Order VIII of the Code requires that denial in the written statement must be specific. It is a cardinal principle of law that material facts must be stated by the parties either in offence or in defense. If a party omits to state a material fact in his pleading, he will not be allowed to lead evidence of that fact at the trial unless the pleading is lawfully amended. Even if, evidence is given on such fact, such evidence must be kept out of the consideration of the Court. Even an argument involving a question of fact which has not been pleaded by the party concerned cannot be allowed at the stage of argument. In spite of clear assertion in the plaint about the written acknowledgments by the defendants, the contesting defendants have not refused these facts in their written statement as a result of which these assertions of the plaintiff stand admitted according to the law of pleading." Learned Advocate lastly relied on decision of Syed Ali Sarder vs Shahabuddin Ahmed Chowdhury, 18 DLR 198, where the Court after considering para 2 of the plaint, where it has been stated that the Khatian No. 14 recording raiyati interest of Nauarraja was a collusive one and that Naurraja had no raiyati right in the Khatian No. 14 and that he did not pay any rent for such raiyati holding, it was contended that it was averred in paragraph 2 of the plaint that the raiyati recorded in the name of Naurraja was a collusive one who had in fact no such interest. In the written statement there was no specific denial of the statement. There is only a general denial in the written statement to the effect that defendants do not admit what was stated in paragraphs 1 to 3 of the plaint. On this basis it was argued that this would amount to denial of the statement in the plaint that the Khatian was wrong, it was held that "this contention cannot be accepted in view of the provision of Order VIII, rules 3 and 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
